_about: Fixed medicine-safety knowledge base for DOC. This is not generated by an LLM. Keys in food_notes and 'generics' lists are the generic ids from medicines.json. 'classes' lists use the 'class' values from medicines.json. An interaction applies when the person takes one medicine from each side. With 'classes', the two medicines must be different generics. A rule like ["nsaid","nsaid"] means two different medicines of the same class. A rule may use 'generics', 'classes', or both as 'left'/'right' sides. Every note says 'may' and points to a doctor or pharmacist. Notes never tell anyone to start, stop or change a medicine. In lab_cautions, the rule applies if the person takes any listed generic or any medicine of a listed class AND the latest value of 'test' (code from lab_tests.json) is flagged 'condition' (low/high). Kidney (eGFR) rules and routine monitoring are in medicines.json and are not repeated here. Placeholders in duplicate_note: {brand_a}, {brand_b}, {generic}; in same_class_note: {class}.
disclaimer: General information only. Never stop or change a medicine without your doctor.

metformin.text: Usually taken with or just after meals. This can reduce stomach upset.
Drinking a lot of alcohol while on metformin may raise the risk of a rare but serious problem (lactic acidosis) and of low sugar. Worth discussing with your doctor.

glimepiride.text: Usually taken with breakfast or the first main meal. Skipping meals after taking it may cause low sugar.
Alcohol may increase the chance of low blood sugar. Signs include shaking, sweating, hunger and confusion.

sitagliptin.text: Can be taken with or without food.

vildagliptin.text: Can be taken with or without food.

amlodipine.text: Can be taken with or without food, at about the same time each day.
Large amounts of grapefruit or grapefruit juice may raise amlodipine levels. Grapefruit is not common in India. Other citrus like orange and mosambi is not known to do this.
amlodipine.source: FDA label (amlodipine); Bailey DG et al., CMAJ 2013 (grapefruit-drug interactions)

cilnidipine.text: Large amounts of grapefruit juice may raise the level of this type of BP medicine. Grapefruit is not common in India.
cilnidipine.source: Japanese package insert (cilnidipine): grapefruit juice precaution

telmisartan.text: Salt substitutes and 'low-sodium' salts often contain potassium. With this medicine they may raise potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor before using them.

losartan.text: Salt substitutes and 'low-sodium' salts often contain potassium. With this medicine they may raise potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor before using them.

ramipril.text: Salt substitutes and 'low-sodium' salts often contain potassium. With this medicine they may raise potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor before using them.
Alcohol may make you feel more dizzy or light-headed with this medicine.

enalapril.text: Salt substitutes and 'low-sodium' salts often contain potassium. With this medicine they may raise potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor before using them.

bisoprolol.text: Can be taken with or without food, usually in the morning.
Alcohol may increase dizziness or tiredness with this medicine.

metoprolol.text: Usually taken with or just after a meal, the same way each day.
Alcohol may increase dizziness or tiredness with this medicine.

furosemide.text: Often taken in the morning so that you do not need to pass urine at night.
In hot weather, or with loose motions or vomiting, you may lose too much water. Worth discussing with your doctor how much to drink.

torsemide.text: Often taken in the morning so that you do not need to pass urine at night.
In hot weather, or with loose motions or vomiting, you may lose too much water. Worth discussing with your doctor how much to drink.

spironolactone.text: Salt substitutes, 'low-sodium' salts and potassium supplements may raise potassium too much with this medicine. Worth discussing with your doctor before using them.
Best taken the same way each day, either always with food or always without.

atorvastatin.text: Can be taken at any time of day, with or without food.
Large amounts of grapefruit juice (more than about 1.2 litres a day) may raise atorvastatin levels and the risk of muscle problems. Grapefruit is not common in India.
atorvastatin.source: FDA label (atorvastatin), Drug interactions: grapefruit juice

atorvastatin.text: Drinking a lot of alcohol may add to the liver strain. Worth discussing with your doctor.

rosuvastatin.text: Can be taken at any time of day, with or without food.
Antacid gels or syrups (aluminium/magnesium type) may reduce how much rosuvastatin is absorbed. The label suggests taking the antacid at least 2 hours after rosuvastatin. Ask your pharmacist.

aspirin.text: Usually taken with or just after food. This may reduce stomach upset.
Alcohol may raise the risk of stomach bleeding with aspirin.
aspirin.source: NHS: Low-dose aspirin; FDA OTC label warning (alcohol)

levothyroxine.text: Usually taken on an empty stomach with water, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, at the same time each day.
Calcium and iron tablets may block absorption. They are usually taken at least 4 hours apart from the thyroid tablet.
Tea, coffee or milk taken right after the tablet may reduce absorption. Waiting 30 to 60 minutes is often advised.
levothyroxine.source: FDA label (levothyroxine): take with water only; Benvenga S et al., Thyroid 2008 (coffee)

levothyroxine.text: Soya products and very high-fibre meals may change absorption. Try to keep your diet steady and get TSH checked as advised.

pantoprazole.text: Usually taken before a meal, often before breakfast.

omeprazole.text: Usually taken before a meal, often before breakfast.

aceclofenac.text: Usually taken with or after food. This may reduce stomach irritation.
Alcohol may increase the risk of stomach bleeding with painkillers of this type.
aceclofenac.source: BNF NSAIDs; FDA NSAID class labeling

aceclofenac.text: Drink enough water. When you are dehydrated (fever, loose motions, heat), these painkillers may be harder on the kidneys.
aceclofenac.source: NICE CKS: NSAIDs prescribing issues; KDIGO 2012 AKI

ibuprofen.text: Usually taken with or after food. This may reduce stomach irritation.
Alcohol may increase the risk of stomach bleeding with ibuprofen.
ibuprofen.source: NHS: Ibuprofen; FDA OTC label warning

ibuprofen.text: Drink enough water. When you are dehydrated (fever, loose motions, heat), these painkillers may be harder on the kidneys.
ibuprofen.source: NICE CKS: NSAIDs prescribing issues; KDIGO 2012 AKI

diclofenac.text: Usually taken with or after food. This may reduce stomach irritation.
Alcohol may increase the risk of stomach bleeding with diclofenac.
Drink enough water. When you are dehydrated (fever, loose motions, heat), these painkillers may be harder on the kidneys.
diclofenac.source: NICE CKS: NSAIDs prescribing issues; KDIGO 2012 AKI

paracetamol.text: Can be taken with or without food.
Regular heavy drinking (3 or more drinks a day) with paracetamol may raise the risk of liver damage. Worth discussing with your doctor.
Many cold and pain products also contain paracetamol. Check labels so you do not take it twice by mistake.

ferrous.text: Iron is absorbed better with vitamin C-rich foods like amla, guava, orange, lemon or tomato.
ferrous.source: NHS: Iron deficiency anaemia; ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines 2024

ferrous.text: Tea, coffee, milk and calcium tablets may reduce iron absorption. Taking them 1 to 2 hours apart from iron is often advised.
ferrous.source: NHS: Ferrous sulfate; ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines 2024

ferrous.text: Iron can make stools dark or black. Black, sticky, tarry stools with tummy pain or dizziness need a doctor urgently.

calcium_d3.text: Calcium carbonate tablets are usually absorbed better with a meal.
calcium_d3.source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements: Calcium fact sheet

calcium_d3.text: Keep calcium apart from iron tablets and thyroid tablets (often by at least 4 hours from thyroid tablets). Ask your pharmacist about timing.
calcium_d3.source: FDA label (levothyroxine); NIH ODS: Calcium fact sheet

pregabalin.text: Can be taken with or without food.
Alcohol may increase drowsiness and dizziness. Take care with driving.

dextromethorphan.text: Alcohol may increase drowsiness and dizziness with cough syrups like this.

_unmapped.note: Keep green leafy vegetable (vitamin K) intake steady. Many interactions (NSAIDs, aspirin, antibiotics). Not in medicines.json.
Omeprazole/esomeprazole may reduce its effect (FDA label); with NSAIDs may raise bleeding. Not in medicines.json.
Same clopidogrel interaction as omeprazole. Not in medicines.json.
Beta-blockers may hide low-sugar warning signs; alcohol may cause low sugar. Not in medicines.json.
May raise atorvastatin levels (muscle damage risk). Not in medicines.json.
Alcohol and pregabalin may increase drowsiness and slow breathing. Not in medicines.json.
With ACE inhibitors/ARBs/spironolactone may cause high potassium. Not in medicines.json (handled via food_notes on salt substitutes).

interactions.text: You may be taking two painkillers of the same type (NSAIDs), for example in two different brands. Together they may raise the risk of stomach bleeding and kidney harm without giving better pain relief. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: BNF Appendix 1 (NSAIDs); NICE CKS: NSAIDs prescribing issues

interactions.text: Taking an NSAID painkiller with aspirin may raise the risk of bleeding, especially in the stomach. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: BNF Appendix 1; Stockley's Drug Interactions; FDA NSAID class labeling

interactions.text: Ibuprofen taken regularly may reduce the heart-protecting effect of low-dose aspirin. Timing may matter. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: FDA Science Paper / Information for Healthcare Professionals: Concomitant use of ibuprofen and aspirin (2006)

interactions.text: NSAID painkillers may make this BP medicine work less well, and together they may strain the kidneys, especially in older adults or when dehydrated. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: BNF Appendix 1; NICE CKS: NSAIDs prescribing issues

interactions.text: NSAID painkillers may make this BP medicine work less well, and together they may strain the kidneys, especially in older adults or when dehydrated. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: BNF Appendix 1; NICE CKS: NSAIDs prescribing issues

interactions.text: NSAID painkillers may make water tablets work less well and may strain the kidneys. The risk may be higher if a BP medicine like an ACE inhibitor or ARB is also taken. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: BNF Appendix 1; Stockley's Drug Interactions ('triple whammy' AKI risk); NICE CKS

interactions.text: NSAID painkillers with spironolactone may raise potassium and strain the kidneys. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.

This BP medicine (ACE inhibitor) with spironolactone may raise blood potassium, sometimes to unsafe levels. Doctors often use them together but check potassium and kidney tests regularly. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: BNF Appendix 1; FDA label (spironolactone); Juurlink DN et al., NEJM 2004

interactions.text: This BP medicine (ARB) with spironolactone may raise blood potassium, sometimes to unsafe levels. Doctors often use them together but check potassium and kidney tests regularly. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.

Taking an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together may raise the risk of high potassium, low BP and kidney problems. Guidelines usually advise against this combination. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: NICE NG136 (Hypertension); FDA Drug Safety Communication on dual RAS blockade (2014); ONTARGET trial, NEJM 2008

interactions.text: Beta-blockers may hide some warning signs of low sugar, such as a fast heartbeat or shaking. Sweating and hunger usually still happen. Check sugar if you feel unwell. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
Taking a gliptin with glimepiride may raise the chance of low blood sugar. Your doctor may review the doses. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
Calcium tablets may block the thyroid tablet from being absorbed if taken together. They are usually taken at least 4 hours apart. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: FDA label (levothyroxine); Singh N et al., JAMA 2000

interactions.text: Iron tablets may block the thyroid tablet from being absorbed if taken together. They are usually taken at least 4 hours apart. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: FDA label (levothyroxine); Campbell NR et al., Ann Intern Med 1992

interactions.text: Long-term acid-reducing tablets may reduce how well the thyroid tablet is absorbed. Your doctor may check TSH more often. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: FDA label (levothyroxine), Drug interactions: proton pump inhibitors

interactions.text: Calcium may reduce how much iron is absorbed if both are taken at the same time. Taking them at different times of day is often advised. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: NHS: Ferrous sulfate; NIH ODS: Iron fact sheet

interactions.text: Long-term acid-reducing tablets may reduce how well iron tablets are absorbed. If your haemoglobin is not improving, this is worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: NIH ODS: Iron fact sheet; Lam JR et al., Gastroenterology 2017

interactions.text: Both may cause drowsiness and dizziness. Together the effect may add up, so take care with driving and falls. Worth discussing with your doctor or pharmacist.
interactions.source: FDA label (pregabalin): CNS depressants; BNF Appendix 1

same_class_note.text: Two of your medicines seem to be the same type ({class}). Doctors rarely use two of the same type together. This may be a mix-up between an old and a new prescription. Worth checking with your doctor or pharmacist. Do not stop either one on your own.

duplicate_note: {brand_a} and {brand_b} both contain the same medicine ({generic}). Taking both may mean you get a double dose by mistake. Please check with your doctor or pharmacist before your next dose. Do not stop or change any medicine on your own.

lab_cautions.text: Your potassium is high. You take a BP medicine (ACE inhibitor or ARB) that can raise potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor soon. Do not stop the medicine on your own.
lab_cautions.source: KDIGO 2021 BP in CKD; FDA labels (ACE inhibitors/ARBs)

lab_cautions.text: Your potassium is high. Spironolactone can raise potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor soon. Do not stop the medicine on your own.
Your potassium is low. Water tablets like this can lower potassium. Worth discussing with your doctor.
Your sodium is low. Water tablets can sometimes lower sodium, especially in older adults. Worth discussing with your doctor. Get urgent help if there is confusion, severe weakness or a fit.

Your fasting sugar is low. Glimepiride can cause low sugar. Worth discussing with your doctor soon. If you feel shaky or sweaty, take some sugar or juice. If the person is very confused or cannot swallow, call 112.
lab_cautions.source: FDA label (glimepiride); ADA Standards of Care (hypoglycaemia)

lab_cautions.text: Your haemoglobin is low. You take a medicine (NSAID painkiller or aspirin) that can sometimes cause slow bleeding from the stomach. Worth discussing with your doctor. Black or tarry stools need urgent care.
lab_cautions.source: FDA NSAID class labeling (GI bleeding); BNF

lab_cautions.text: Your platelet count is low. With aspirin or NSAID painkillers, the chance of bleeding may be higher. Worth discussing with your doctor before your next dose.
lab_cautions.source: BNF (NSAIDs, aspirin): caution in bleeding disorders

lab_cautions.text: Your ALT (liver test) is high. Statins can sometimes raise liver tests. Worth discussing with your doctor. Do not stop the medicine on your own.
lab_cautions.source: FDA labels (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin), Warnings: liver enzyme abnormalities

lab_cautions.text: Your ALT (liver test) is high and you take paracetamol. High doses or long use can strain the liver. Worth discussing with your doctor what is safe for you.
lab_cautions.source: FDA: Acetaminophen and liver injury; BNF

lab_cautions.text: Your calcium is high and you take a calcium and vitamin D supplement. Worth discussing with your doctor whether you still need it. Do not change it on your own.
lab_cautions.source: NIH ODS: Calcium and Vitamin D fact sheets

lab_cautions.text: Your TSH is low while on thyroid tablets. This can indicate the current dose is more than you need. Worth discussing with your doctor. Do not change the dose on your own.
lab_cautions.source: ATA guidelines for hypothyroidism 2014; FDA label (levothyroxine)

lab_cautions.text: Your TSH is high while on thyroid tablets. This can happen if the tablet is taken with food, calcium or iron, or if doses are missed. Worth discussing with your doctor.
lab_cautions.source: ATA guidelines for hypothyroidism 2014; FDA label (levothyroxine)

lab_cautions.text: Your ferritin (iron store) is high while taking iron tablets. Worth discussing with your doctor whether you still need them.
lab_cautions.source: NHS: Iron deficiency anaemia; NIH ODS: Iron fact sheet
